title: Knight Hops on a Keypad
statement:
A phone keypad has four rows: 1 2 3, 4 5 6, 7 8 9, and * 0 #. A chess knight stands on a key of your choice and then makes jumps. A jump is the usual knight move: two keys in one direction and one key sideways. The knight may only stand on digit keys; * and # are off limits.

The knight writes down every digit it stands on, including the first one. Return how many different digit strings of length n it can write, that is, with exactly n − 1 jumps. The count grows fast, so return it modulo 1 000 000 007.

examples.why: For example 1 → 6 → 0, 4 → 3 → 8, 0 → 4 → 9. Keys 4 and 6 have three exits, the 5 key has none, the rest have two.
No jump at all. Every digit key is a valid start, including 5, even though the knight could never leave it.
Not 46 · 2 or any fixed multiple: how many strings continue depends on which key they end on.

hints: Write down, for every digit, which digits a knight can reach from it in one jump. Note that 5 reaches nothing and nothing reaches 5.
Let ways[d] be the number of strings of the current length that end on digit d. How do you get the counts for one more digit?
next[d] is the sum of ways[p] over every digit p that jumps to d. Start with all ones, repeat n − 1 times, sum, and take the modulo at every addition.

explain.intuition:
A string is fully described by its digits, and whether it can continue only depends on its last digit. So group strings by their last digit and count each group. One jump turns the counts for length k into the counts for length k + 1: every string ending on p continues to each neighbour of p.

The reachability table is small and fixed: 0 ↔ 4, 6; 1 ↔ 6, 8; 2 ↔ 7, 9; 3 ↔ 4, 8; 4 ↔ 0, 3, 9; 6 ↔ 0, 1, 7; 7 ↔ 2, 6; 8 ↔ 1, 3; 9 ↔ 2, 4; and 5 is isolated. The whole problem is 10 counters updated n − 1 times. Symmetry shrinks it further: the four corners behave alike, as do 2 and 8, and 4 and 6.
steps: Write the neighbour list for each digit.
Set ways[d] = 1 for all ten digits (strings of length 1).
Repeat n − 1 times: next[d] = Σ ways[p] over neighbours p of d, modulo 1 000 000 007.
pitfalls: Leaving out 5 for n = 1. A single digit needs no jump, so the answer is 10, not 9.
Taking the modulo only at the end. The counts grow by a factor of about 2.3 per step and overflow long before n = 5000.
Multiplying the total by the average number of exits. The count per ending key differs, and those differences change the next step.

solutions.title: Explore every path
solutions.idea: From each start, try every jump recursively and count the strings of length n.

solutions.title: Counts per ending digit
solutions.idea: Keep how many strings end on each digit; one jump redistributes those counts to the neighbours.

solutions.title: Four symmetry groups
solutions.idea: Corners (1, 3, 7, 9), the middle column (2, 8), the side keys (4, 6) and 0 behave alike within a group. Track four totals instead of ten.

followups: n can be 10¹⁸. The step is a fixed linear map, so how does fast matrix exponentiation give O(log n)?
Return how many strings start and end on the same digit.
